name: Battle of Mikatagahara
info: Takeda Shingen's army overran Tokugawa Ieyasu and his Oda allies on the plain of Mikatagahara in Tōtōmi Province on 25 January 1573, while Shingen marched towards Kyoto; Ieyasu escaped to Hamamatsu, and Shingen turned back.

facts.date: 25 January 1573; in the Japanese calendar the 22nd day of the 12th month of the 3rd year of Genki
facts.place: The plain of Mikatagahara, north of Hamamatsu, in Tōtōmi Province, in present-day Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan
facts.sides: The Takeda under Takeda Shingen, who led 30,000 men south in October 1572 while Yamagata Masakage led a second force of 5,000 into eastern Mikawa; the Tokugawa under Tokugawa Ieyasu, with 8,000 men at Hamamatsu Castle plus 3,000 reinforcements from Oda Nobunaga. The Kōyō Gunkan says Shingen outnumbered Ieyasu three to one.
facts.outcome: The Tokugawa and Oda force was almost totally destroyed and many of Ieyasu's retainers were killed. Ieyasu escaped to Hamamatsu Castle with five men, and a night attack by his remaining men helped persuade Shingen to withdraw.

t: Ieyasu fought on the plain against the advice of his own generals and of the Oda officers sent to help him, although Shingen had wished to avoid conflict and save his forces for Oda Nobunaga.

Tokugawa arquebusiers opened the battle, but Takeda cavalry rapidly overran Honda Tadakatsu's segment on the Tokugawa right, and a second cavalry charge followed by the Takeda main body drove the Tokugawa army into disorderly retreat.
Ieyasu returned to Hamamatsu with only five men and ordered the gates left open and braziers lit; the Takeda vanguard took this for a trap and camped for the night.
dyk: When Ieyasu reached Hamamatsu Castle, he is said to have ordered the gates left open and braziers lit, while Sakai Tadatsugu beat a large war drum. The Takeda vanguard took it for a trap and stopped to make camp.
ev: Aoyama Tadamon, a vassal of Ieyasu, resists the Takeda invasion of Mikawa and is later killed by a gunshot
Shingen leads 30,000 men south from Kōfu into Tōtōmi while Yamagata Masakage leads 5,000 into eastern Mikawa, and they take Yoshida Castle and Futamata Castle
The Tokugawa vanguard meets Yamagata Masakage and Baba Nobuharu at the Battle of Hitokotosaka
Ieyasu draws up his forces on the plain of Mikatagahara, and Takeda cavalry overrun the Tokugawa right and the Oda reinforcements
A second Takeda cavalry charge and the Takeda main body drive the Tokugawa army into retreat, and Ieyasu flees to Hamamatsu
That night about 100 Tokugawa foot soldiers and 16 matchlock gunners attack the Takeda camp and Shingen decides to withdraw
Shingen is fatally wounded at the Siege of Noda Castle

sections.background:
In 1571 Aoyama Tadamon, a vassal of Tokugawa Ieyasu, resisted a Takeda invasion of Mikawa by way of Asuke Castle, building a series of palisades to thwart the early incursion. He later drove the Takeda back at Shinpukuji, north of Dōdo Castle, but was killed in a battle by a gunshot and succeeded by his son Aoyama Tadanari.

In October 1572 Takeda Shingen made a larger move. He had concluded alliances with his rivals to the east, the Later Hōjō clan of Odawara and the Satomi clan of Awa, and had waited for the snow to close the northern mountain passes against his northern rival Uesugi Kenshin. He then led 30,000 men south from his capital at Kōfu into Tōtōmi Province, while Yamagata Masakage led a second force of 5,000 into eastern Mikawa. They quickly captured Yoshida Castle and Futamata Castle.

Shingen was campaigning against Oda Nobunaga and seeking a route from Kōfu to Kyoto. His intent was not to attack Ieyasu or to seize Hamamatsu; he wished to avoid conflict if possible, to save his forces for Nobunaga and the march on Kyoto. Ieyasu was based at Hamamatsu Castle. In the same month he sent Naitō Nobunari, Honda Tadakatsu and Ōkubo Tadasuke to lead the vanguard, which met Takeda forces under Yamagata Masakage and Baba Nobuharu at the Battle of Hitokotosaka. Tadakatsu and Nobunari fought well and broke through the Takeda attempts to encircle them.
sections.forces:
Shingen led 30,000 men into Tōtōmi, and Yamagata Masakage led a separate force of 5,000 into eastern Mikawa. Ieyasu was at Hamamatsu Castle with 8,000 men, plus 3,000 reinforcements received from his ally Oda Nobunaga. The Kōyō Gunkan, a record of the Takeda family's military exploits, says that Shingen outnumbered Ieyasu three to one.

According to the same record, Shingen organised his men in the gyorin, or fish-scale, formation, to entice his opponent to attack. Oyamada Nobushige was in the vanguard, followed by Naitō Masatoyo and Yamagata Masakage. The third line was commanded by Katsuyori and Obata Masamori, and Baba Nobuharu was in the fourth. Opposing him, Ieyasu had gathered his available forces and arrayed them in a line.

Ieyasu's decision to fight was not shared by his advisers. Sakuma Nobumori and Takigawa Kazumasu, who had been sent by Nobunaga, and his own generals Matsudaira Koretada and Ishikawa Kazumasa advised against it. Ieyasu nevertheless refused to let the Takeda pass through his territory unhindered and drew up his forces on a high plain called Mikatagahara, then just north of Hamamatsu. The historian Kawai Atsushi viewed the decision as a necessity rather than a gamble: the Mikawa samurai clans were aggressive and proud, and if Ieyasu had refused to fight the invaders he would have lost their respect and weakened his control of the province.
sections.course:
At around four in the afternoon, as snow began to fall, Tokugawa arquebusiers accompanied by a number of peasant stone-throwers opened fire on the Takeda formation. Ieyasu had expected his firearms to overcome Shingen's much larger force. The expectation was quickly dispelled: Naitō Masatoyo's vanguard cavalry attacked and rapidly overran Honda Tadakatsu's segment on the Tokugawa right. Takeda horsemen exploited the opening, assaulted the Oda reinforcements and charged the Tokugawa rear. The Oda forces were routed, the officer Hirate Hirohide was killed, and Sakuma Nobumori and Takigawa Kazumasu fled. A similar attack on the left was thwarted, because the Tokugawa units there refused to yield ground, and an encirclement of the Tokugawa centre was prevented.

Shingen then withdrew his vanguard to rest and brought forward fresh horsemen from the main body, ordering Takeda Katsuyori, Obata Masamori and Saegusa Moritomo to lead a two-pronged cavalry charge into the weakening Tokugawa line. The foot-soldier-heavy Takeda main body followed closely, and their combined weight drove the battered Tokugawa army into a disorderly retreat.

Ieyasu ordered Ōkubo Tadayo to plant his golden fan standard on a hill and rally the troops towards the castle town of Saigadake. He then sought to re-engage the Takeda in person, to free his trapped general Mizuno Tadashige, but his retainer Natsume Yoshinobu persuaded him to retreat. Convinced that as head of the clan his life was too important, Ieyasu fled the field. To buy time, Natsume Yoshinobu led the few soldiers left under his command in a suicide charge against the advancing Takeda and was killed.
sections.aftermath:
Other notable Tokugawa retainers killed in the fighting were Matsudaira Koretada, Naruse Masayoshi, Toyama Kosaku and Endo Ukon, whose units were encircled and overrun by the Takeda forces. The Tokugawa and Oda force was almost totally destroyed. When Ieyasu returned to Hamamatsu Castle he was accompanied by only five men, and the town was on the verge of panic, as rumour had already reached it that the battle had gone badly.

Ieyasu commanded that the castle gates remain open and that braziers be lit to guide his retreating army to safety, and Sakai Tadatsugu beat a large war drum to persuade the returning men of their courageous retreat. The Takeda vanguard under Baba Nobuharu and Yamagata Masakage heard the drums and saw the braziers and open gates. They assumed that Ieyasu had planned a trap and stopped to make camp for the night where they stood, short of Hamamatsu.

In the night a small band of about 100 Tokugawa foot soldiers and 16 matchlock gunners, led by Ōkubo Tadayo and Amano Yasukage, attacked the Takeda camp and threw the vanguard into confusion. Uncertain of the remaining strength of the Tokugawa, and worried that reinforcements from Oda Nobunaga or Uesugi Kenshin were on their way, Shingen decided to withdraw to his own territories. The skirmish took place near Saigagake, a narrow gorge about ten metres deep and 450 metres long, about one kilometre north of Hamamatsu Castle. There was to be no following attack on Hamamatsu: Shingen was fatally wounded in February 1573 at the Siege of Noda Castle and died in May 1573.
sections.sources:
The Kōyō Gunkan, a record of the Takeda family's military exploits, is the source for the Takeda order of battle and for the claim that Shingen outnumbered Ieyasu three to one and drew up his army in the gyorin formation. It is a record kept by the Takeda family, the winning side.

Some of the best-known episodes of the night after the battle come from later sources. The Kansei Chōshū Shokafu, a genealogy of the major samurai families compiled by the later Tokugawa shogunate, records that the Iga ninja Hattori Hanzō rendered meritorious service at Mikatagahara: he captured a Takeda spy named Chikuan and delayed the advancing Takeda at the Tenryū River with a counterattack of only thirty men.

The story of the Battle of Saigagake, as it is known in Japanese sources, is likewise an anecdote. In it the Tokugawa stretched a cloth across the cliff to look like a bridge, and the Takeda suffered numerous casualties trying to flee across it. This account appears in later records compiled by the Tokugawa shogunate and not in contemporary historical records, although the site of the alleged ruse was designated a Shizuoka Prefecture Historic Site in 1952.
sections.legacy:
The Battle of Mikatagahara was one of the most famous battles of Takeda Shingen's campaigns and one of the most notable demonstrations of cavalry tactics of the Sengoku period. It was also Tokugawa Ieyasu's most decisive defeat: his army was effectively annihilated, and he himself escaped death only narrowly, through a bluff and a perilous night attack.

The battle's effect on the campaign was limited by Shingen's own fate. His march towards Kyoto, which had begun in October 1572 as a campaign against Oda Nobunaga, did not continue. He was fatally wounded in February 1573 at the Siege of Noda Castle and died in May 1573, so there was no following attack on Hamamatsu.

The episode of the open gates, the braziers and the war drum, and the tales of Natsume Yoshinobu's charge and of Saigagake, belong to the way the battle has been told. The site of the alleged Saigagake ruse is a Shizuoka Prefecture Historic Site, designated in 1952. The historian Kawai Atsushi's reading, that Ieyasu fought because he needed to keep the respect of the Mikawa samurai clans, offers a reason why Ieyasu fought a far larger army against the advice of others.

summary: On 25 January 1573 Takeda Shingen's army, marching towards Kyoto, overran Tokugawa Ieyasu and his Oda allies on the plain of Mikatagahara. Ieyasu escaped to Hamamatsu with five men, and Shingen withdrew after a night attack; he died in May 1573.
notes: The article is thin: it gives no casualty figures for either side. Strengths are 30,000 plus 5,000 for the Takeda, 8,000 plus 3,000 for the Tokugawa and Oda; the three-to-one ratio is the Kōyō Gunkan's, a Takeda record.

The article's lead and aftermath say the Tokugawa-Oda force was 'almost totally annihilated' and 'effectively annihilated'; I wrote 'almost totally destroyed' and 'effectively annihilated' only in the legacy as the article's wording.
The article does not say who won the night skirmish nor what Takeda losses were; the Saigagake cloth-bridge ruse is stated by the article to be a later anecdote.
Hitokotosaka is dated only 'in the same month' as the October 1572 advance, so I gave it as October 1572.

Left out: nothing of substance; the article has no information on the field's layout beyond 'high plain north of Hamamatsu', on Tokugawa strength after the battle, or on later memory beyond the 1952 designation.
